title: In the Valley of Elah
full_review:
The title of the metaphorically named "In the Valley of Elah" (Warner Independent) refers (in case you're not up on your Bible geography) to the locale where David fought Goliath.

Inspired by true events as related in a Playboy magazine story -- "Death and Dishonor" by Mark Boal -- the film is a powerfully understated drama about a patriotic ex-military man, Hank Deerfield (Tommy Lee Jones), who, leaving his worried wife, Joan (Susan Sarandon), at home, travels from Tennessee to New Mexico to search for their missing son, Mike, a solider who's just returned from duty in Iraq, only to come up against the military bureaucracy.

As a respected former officer, Hank is welcomed warmly at the military base from which his son has gone missing, but at first learns nothing significant. The most substantial clues to Mike's whereabouts come from the cell phone Hank purloins from a drawer in Mike's quarters on base, which turns out to have some cryptic but disturbing images of Iraq, which are extracted by a computer hacker he hires. These are unveiled slowly throughout the film for maximum dramatic effect.

He joins forces with police detective Emily Sanders (Charlize Theron), a single mom who holds her own in the macho world of her police unit. She blows him off at first, telling him it's a military matter, but eventually when the case appears to be in civil jurisdiction, they work to break through the red tape of the military -- Lt. Kirklander (Jason Patric) is the most immediate obstacle there -- and her own police force, as they begin to suspect foul play.

There's no romantic involvement whatsoever, but Hank becomes close to Emily, and bonds with her young son, to whom he actually recounts the story of David and Goliath.

It would spoil the intricate plot to say more. Suffice it to say, after he interrogates Hank's buddies -- Steve Penning (Wes Chatham), Gordon Bonner (Jake McLaughlin), Robert Oritez (Victor Wolf) and Ennis Long (Mehcad Brooks) -- what Hank learns of his son's service in Iraq is profoundly disillusioning, to put it mildly.

The film plays beautifully as a mystery with sustained suspense, but writer-director Paul Haggis's script ultimately delivers a strong anti-war message, and cast members -- who also include James Franco and Josh Brolin on the military and police sides, respectively -- give sensitive, nuanced performances. Jones is masterful in conveying the unwavering conviction of a father who's already lost one son to the military and is determined not to lose the other. Theron is wonderfully unshowy as a decent officer, trying to do her job despite constant heckling from her colleagues.

At one point, Hank must go to a men's club, a soldier's hangout, and there are some topless pole dancers. Later, he encounters Evie, a topless waitress of a certain age, played with no-nonsense empathy by Frances Fisher. She returns (fully clothed) later on, disclosing that she saw Mike the night he disappeared.

The film works as entertainment and conveys its anti-war message without being unpatriotic or heavy-handed. Its subtlety and balance make it well worth seeing.

The film contains rough language and profanity, rear shower nudity, upper female nudity, brief gruesome war and morgue imagery and verbal descriptions, suicide, drug references and a violent scuffle. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
